items.meaning: It's okay / I'm fine / No thank you (declining politely)
Just a moment / Excuse me (to get past or to pause someone)
Excuse me (to get a stranger's attention; literally 'over there')
No / Not at all (also the usual reply to thanks or an apology)
Excuse me! (calling staff in a restaurant)
This one, please (pointing at a menu or item)
I'm not sure / I don't really know
Goodbye (to someone who is leaving while you stay)
Goodbye (when you leave and the other person stays)
Sorry, what did you say? / What?! (surprised)
Have you eaten? (a friendly greeting, like 'how are you?')
Excuse me (before interrupting, squeezing past or entering)
I know, right? / Exactly (agreeing with what was just said)
Said before eating, thanking whoever made or paid for the meal
Said after eating, thanking whoever made or paid for the meal
How are you doing? / How have you been?
Welcome (said by staff when customers come in)
Why? / What is it? (when someone calls you)
How is it? / How about it?
How many people? (heard at a restaurant door)
Could you say that once more?
I'll take this one / I'll have this
To go, please / Please wrap it up

Do you need a bag? (heard at a checkout)

What time do you close? (literally 'until what time do you do it?')
Could we have more side dishes? (refills are usually free)
Could you take a picture of us?
Can I sit here? / Is this seat free?
In one payment, please (the card terminal asks 일시불 or 할부, installments)
Do you have it in another color?
Where do I transfer? (bus or subway)
Coming through (excuse me, I need to get past)
Where are you now? (on the phone)
I think I'll be a little late
Awesome / Wow (casual slang for something amazing)
No way… / Surely not (expecting it isn't true)
No way / That makes no sense (casual)
Oh dear / Oof (sympathy, tiredness or surprise)
What do I do? / Oh no (casual; polite: 어떡해요)
That's great / I'm glad it worked out
I'm fine / I'm good (often a polite no to an offer)
It doesn't matter / I don't mind
Let's do that / Sure, go ahead
I'll think about it (often a soft no)
Next time (a soft way to say no)
No / You can't / It doesn't work
Don't worry about it / Never mind
That's true / You have a point
May I have your name? (very polite)
How old are you? (polite; age decides how people talk to each other)
How do you say this in Korean?
What did you do on the weekend?
Do you have time? / Are you free?
Let's go together / Come with me
What do you want to eat?
I'll message you on KakaoTalk (Korea's main messaging app)
Let's grab a meal sometime (often a friendly goodbye, not a firm plan)
Get home safely (said when parting in the evening)
Take care getting home / Travel safely
I'll head off first (leaving before others)
Have a good trip / See you when you're back (to someone going out)
I'm off! (said when leaving home or the office for a while)
Enjoy your meal (often said by restaurant staff)
Please eat a lot / Enjoy your meal (said by the host)
Is the food to your taste? (literally 'does it fit your mouth?')
Nice to meet you (formal, first meeting)
I look forward to working with you / Please take care of this (said when starting something together)
You scared me! / What a surprise
I'm in big trouble / This is a disaster
What a waste / So close (regret over a missed chance or waste)
I'm upset / That hurts (disappointed or sad)
I'm jealous / I envy you (usually friendly)
It suits you / They go well together
How cool / That's fascinating (something new or surprising)
It's a hassle / I can't be bothered
I like it (it suits my taste)
You can do it! / Let's go! (encouragement)
I miss you (literally 'I want to see you')
It'll be okay / Things will get better
Take care of yourself (often when someone is ill or travelling)
Said when leaving people who are still working (shop staff, colleagues)
Thank you for your hard work (said at the end of work or a task)
Good work / You must be tired (after something hard)
You've been through a lot / Thank you for all your effort
Excuse me, but… (before a personal question or request)
Sorry, but… (softening a request or interruption)
By the way / Anyway (changing the subject)
That can't be / There's no way that's true
Don't mention it (polite reply to thanks or praise)
Thanks to you (polite reply when asked how things went)
That's enough / Never mind / No thanks (can sound cold)
Can we talk for a minute?
I'll do my best (literally 'I'll work hard')
I'll be leaving first (polite, leaving the office before others)
Happy New Year (literally: receive many blessings)
It's on the house (a free extra from the restaurant or shop)
No onions, please (swap in any ingredient)
Sell a lot! (a friendly goodbye to a shop owner)
I'll treat you (usually to celebrate good news)
Bottoms up (drink it all in one go)
Let's go to a second place (another bar or restaurant after the first)
A team dinner or drinks with colleagues
I'm starving (literally: so hungry I could die)
I'm swamped / My head is all over the place
Please speak casually to me (inviting someone to drop polite speech)
Can I speak casually with you?
I've heard a lot about you
I owe you a lot (thanks for help or hospitality)
It's no joke / It's insane (very good or very bad, casual)
Snap out of it / Get a grip (casual)
Yes! / Woohoo! (casual, when something goes your way)
What did I tell you? / Told you so (casual)
Push and pull in dating (playing hard to get)
To be in a 'something' — mutual interest before officially dating
To fall in love at first sight
To watch others' reactions and act carefully around them
To be quick to read the room / pick up on unspoken cues
To understand each other / click (literally 'words get through')
To grow attached (to a person, place or thing over time)
To take a lot of work (literally 'hands go to it a lot')
To be stunning (amazingly good) or dumbfounding (unbelievably bad)
To know a lot of people; literally 'feet are wide'
To have high standards (in partners, products…)
To be good at keeping secrets; literally 'mouth is heavy'
To be unable to keep secrets; literally 'mouth is light'
To be a picky or light eater; literally 'mouth is short'
To be generous (especially cooking or giving too much); literally 'hand is big'
To be jealous of someone's success (also literally 'stomach hurts')
To clear one's head / take a break
To be easily persuaded; literally 'ears are thin'
To be betrayed; literally 'get hit on the back of the head'
To quit / wash one's hands of something
To fail (an exam or application); literally 'eat seaweed soup'
To pretend not to know / play innocent
To actively step in to help
To be humbled / have one's pride crushed
Can't stop thinking about someone or something (worry or longing)
To be in an urgent situation; literally 'fire falls on the top of your foot'
A piece of cake; literally 'eating rice cake lying down'
Easy as pie; literally 'eating cooled porridge'
Eat first, then everything else; literally 'even Mt. Geumgang is sightseeing after a meal'
Don't count your chickens before they hatch; literally 'don't drink the kimchi soup first'
Pie in the sky / Something you can't have; literally 'rice cake in a picture'
Old habits die hard; literally 'habits at three last until eighty'

items.korean: 가는 말이 고와야 오는 말이 곱다
items.meaning: Be kind to others and they'll be kind to you; literally 'outgoing words must be nice for incoming words to be nice'
Every little bit adds up; literally 'gather dust and make a great mountain'
Even experts make mistakes; literally 'even monkeys fall from trees'
Seeing is believing; literally 'hearing a hundred times is not as good as seeing once'
Many hands make light work; literally 'even a sheet of paper is easier lifted together'
